text: Welcome to week six of the official
NASCAR Gen 4 Cup Series. And this week,
you'll be taking on the Tallaladega
Super Speedway for 50 laps. To get
started in qualifying this week, you
want to keep the tires as cold as
possible. So, shift up to fourth gear
and ease the car out of the pits as
easily as you can. Any sudden bumps,
steering inputs, and acceleration will
add unwanted heat, so be sure to take it
as slow as possible. Get up to 101 mph
to avoid triggering the qualifying
scrutiny and continue rolling until you
hit turns three and four. Keeping the
car in the top lane, you want to slowly
ease onto the gas to begin accelerating.
You can wait even longer to start going,
but I like to stick to turn three just
to be safe. Keep the car in the top
groove, straddling the highest white
line with your left front as you take
your first lap. Stay up there, but don't
let yourself get too close to the wall.
The last thing you need to do is force
air on your spoiler. So, feel free to
run a lane lower if it makes you feel
better. Take the outside and turns to
reinforce as you come around to take the
white flag. My line is kind of awkward
running through the trial here, but it
brought me the best result. You may find
a different route in practice, but as
long as you're getting momentum off of
the banking in the trioval, you should
be set. Point the car into turn one and
run as close to the yellow line as you
can without hitting it. It's easy to
overstep and scrape the veillance on the
apron if you aren't careful. So, be sure
to find a consistent steering angle and
stick to it. Let the car track out
slightly out of the corner, but not so
much that you sacrifice your forward
momentum. Once the car is pointed down
the backstretch, slowly guide the car
down with your eyes on the yellow line
heading into turn three.
Ease back into your preferred steering
angle as you run through the final
corners. As you reach the exit, you want
to allow the car to track up slightly,
but not as much as before. Guide the car
back down to the yellow line as you
enter the trial and give yourself as
straight of a shot to the line as you
can without hitting the apron.
Let's take another look at that lap.

Once the race begins, you'll be starting
firmly in second gear. Wheel spin won't
be a factor this week, but what might
cause problems on the starts and
restarts is people opting to short shift
rather than using their entire
tachometer. While it's true that the
RPMs are limited this week, the worst
thing you can do toward the front of the
field is shift too early as the car bogs
down and hinders the initial momentum of
your line. Keep an eye on your RPM and
shift between 7900 and 8,000.
Once you get the shifting out of the
way, you'll find that this package
rewards the line that gets the better
start. You may have noticed that the
inside got the jump here, and that was a
result of the third car on the outside
not keeping up on the start, forcing all
of the work on the 26 car to keep me in
contact with the leaders. Without help,
the 26 had no choice but to fall back to
the car behind him, waiting the entire
backstretch to get the help he needed to
get back up to me. A few laps later, I
ended up with the 24 car on my bumper,
and the middle lane began to roll. As
this was my first Super Speedway race in
this car, I made the mistake of going to
the inside here. Not only was I too far
out ahead, but I also failed to take
into account that the higher you go up,
the stronger your line can become.
Strength and numbers will ultimately win
in most cases, but if a line of strong
drivers moves up to the outside, it will
be very difficult to overcome them.
As the side draft is still a notable
factor in these cars, this effect is the
same in the middle groove, leaving the
inside especially vulnerable. If you can
manage to break away on the inside, it
would be the strongest place for you to
stay. But if you find yourself among a
pack of cars, you'd be better off in the
higher two lanes. With that being said,
be sure to keep an eye on the cars
around you and make sure that you're
confident in who you'll be working with
before you commit. The higher you move
up the track, the more difficult it
becomes to avoid wrecks. So, be ready to
pick a hill to die on. At long last, we
finally have the super speedway bodies.
But don't let the tall nose give you a
false sense of security when the time
comes to push. The roundness of the nose
can steer the car ahead of you, even if
you're pushing a square. So, you'll have
to be careful. It's the pusher's
responsibility to hold their car
straight during a push. It's the
leader's responsibility to hold their
line and give their pusher a bumper they
can keep up with. If either party makes
a mistake or strays away from their
line, odds are that it'll result in a
crash. So, keep this in mind if you find
yourself close to the front of your
lane.
If you can pick your lines, keep your
car in one piece, and use your bumper
wisely, you could find yourself fighting
for the win in the closing laps. Good
luck.
